catalog_quote: [1964, p. 197, sec. 10.2 शब्द-स्तर, 10.2.1] इस प्रकार के परिवर्तन का उत्तरदायित्व बहुत कुछ स्वराघात पर होता है, यथा—भाण् + ओई = भणोई ( बहनोई), लाल् + आई = ललाई, पाणी + हारो = पणिहारो (पनिहारा) आदि अर्थात् स्वराघात-स्थलों के परिवर्तन से भी शब्दों में ध्वनि-प्रक्रिया देखी जाती है जिसके सम्बन्ध में निम्न नियम बनाये जा सकते हैं— १. दीर्घ-स्वरों का ह्रस्व होना— [1963 thesis, p. 85, sec. 2.7.1] शेखावाटी का वाक्य सुरलहर के किसी विशिष्ट रूप से आच्छादित रहता है । इस सुरलहर के द्वारा वाक्यगत पदों का गठन प्रभावित नहीं होता । अतएव शेखावाटी शब्द या पद सहज सुर नहीं धारण करते । शेखावाटी सुरलहर के मुख्य तीन स्तर हैं - सम, उन्नायक, तथा अवनायक ।
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: [1964, p. 197] इस प्रकार के परिवर्तन का उत्तरदायित्व बहुत कुछ स्वराघात पर होता है, यथा—भाण् + ओई = भणोई (बहनोई), लाल् + आई = ललाई, पाणी + हारो = पणिहारो (पनिहारा) आदि अर्थात् स्वराघात-स्थलों के परिवर्तन से भी शब्दों में ध्वनि-प्रक्रिया देखी जाती है जिसके सम्बन्ध में निम्न नियम बनाये जा सकते हैं— १. दीर्घ-स्वरों का ह्रस्व होना— [1963 thesis, p. 85] इस सुरलहर के द्वारा वाक्यगत पदों का गठन प्रभावित नहीं होता। अतएव शेखावाटी शब्द या पद सहज सुर नहीं धारण करते। शेखावाटी सुरलहर के मुख्य तीन स्तर हैं — सम, उन्नायक, तथा अवनायक।
new_statements.translation: [1964, p. 197] Responsibility for changes of this kind rests largely on the accent (svarāghāt), e.g. bhāṇ + oī = bhaṇoī ('sister's husband'), lāl + āī = lalāī, pāṇī + hāro = paṇihāro ('water-carrier') etc.; that is, a phonological process is also observed in words through the change of accent positions, for which the following rules can be made: 1. shortening of long vowels ... [1963, p. 85] The make-up of the words in a sentence is not affected by this intonation. Hence Shekhawati words or pads do not bear inherent pitch (sur). Shekhawati intonation has three main levels: level, rising and falling.
new_statements.citation: Agrawal, Kailash Chandra & Din Dayalu Gupta. 1964. Śekhāvāṭī bolī kā varṇanātmaka adhyayana. Lucknow: Lucknow University, p. 197 (sec. 10.2.1); and the thesis version, Agarwal, K. C. 1963. A descriptive analysis of Shekhawati dialect. PhD, University of Lucknow (Shodhganga 10603/596328), p. 85 (sec. 2.7.1)
new_statements.locator: 1964 book p. 197, sec. 10.2.1 'shabd-star' (word level), lines 11-14; 1963 thesis p. 85, sec. 2.7.1 'surlahar' (intonation), lines 1-5
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both quoted passages verified on the page images, not just the scanned. (1) Agrawal & Gupta 1964, printed p. 197 = PDF p. 193 : sec. 10.2 'shabd-star', 10.2.1, the passage 'इस प्रकार के परिवर्तन का उत्तरदायित्व बहुत कुछ स्वराघात पर होता है, यथा—भाण् + ओई = भणोई (बहनोई), लाल् + आई = ललाई, पाणी + हारो = पणिहारो (पनिहारा) आदि अर्थात् स्वराघात-स्थलों के परिवर्तन से भी शब्दों में ध्वनि-प्रक्रिया देखी जाती है जिसके सम्बन्ध में निम्न नियम बनाये जा सकते हैं— १. दीर्घ-स्वरों का ह्रस्व होना—' is there word for word (archive.org djvu the scanned textgarble a few aksharas; the image is clean). What follows on pp. 197-198 is only the vowel-shortening rules (ā>a, ī/e/ai>i) with examples; no statement of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given. The 1963/64 description recognizes intonation, juncture and nasality as the suprasegmentals of Shekhawati and has no stress section; it states that words carry no inherent pitch. The only word-level accent remark (p. 197) is that when a suffix with a long vowel is added the accent position changes and the base's long vowel shortens (bhāṇ > bhaṇ-oī, lāl > lal-āī, pāṇī > paṇi-hāro), which is consistent with the accent going to the last long vowel of the derived word, but the authors do not say so.
new_statements.exceptions: None; 'balaghat (Stress)' on pp. 178-179 and sec. 6.6 (p. 107) refers only to sentence-level emphasis (scrambled word order, emphatic particles ī, bī, to, tak).
new_statements.domain_note: p. 197 remark is about derived/compound words at 'shabd-star' (word level); p. 85 is about sentence intonation vs. word pitch. Variety = Shekhawati of Sikar-Jhunjhunu-Churu (the author's mother tongue; regional forms in sec. 1.5).
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Shekhawati proper (shek1243; Sikar, Jhunjhunu, Churu districts; dialects sika1258 Sikar and jhun1238 Jhunjhunu-Churu), the author's mother tongue in the 1963/64 work. Grierson 1908 treats it as 'Northern Marwari' together with Bikaneri and Bagri (bagr1243); the Bagri stress rule in Gusain 1999 is NOT a Shekhawati statement.

new_statements.quote: उपर्युक्त सभी प्रकार के वाक्यों में बलाघात (Stress) का समावेश भी हो सकता है। प्रश्नवाचक पद तो बलाघात प्रधान होते ही हैं, उनके अभाव में आवश्यकतानुसार अन्य पदों को भी बलाघात का पुट प्रदान किया जा सकता है। यथा— मैं घरां जाऊँ = क्या मैं घर को जाऊँ? [written three times, the stress mark under जाऊँ, घरां and मैं in turn] उपर्युक्त वाक्यों में क्रमशः 'जाने', 'घर' (जाने) तथा 'स्वयं को' (घर जाने) की अनुमति मांगी गई है। ... इस प्रकार शेखावाटी में सुरलहर के आधार पर संघटित वाक्य तीन कोटि के ही माने जा सकते हैं — सामान्य, प्रश्नवाचक, और विस्मय-बोधक।
new_statements.translation: In all the above kinds of sentence, stress (balāghāt) may also be brought in. Interrogative words are stress-bearing by nature; in their absence other words too may be given a tinge of stress as required, e.g. maĩ gharã̄ jāũ 'Shall I go home?' [three times, stress marked under jāũ 'go', gharã̄ 'home' and maĩ 'I' in turn]. In these sentences permission is asked, respectively, for going, for (going) home, and for (I) myself (going home). ... Thus, on the basis of intonation, Shekhawati sentences fall into only three classes: plain, interrogative and exclamatory.
new_statements.citation: Agarwal, K. C. 1963. A descriptive analysis of Shekhawati dialect. PhD, University of Lucknow — remaining bitstreams (05_chapter 1, 07_chapter 3, 08_chapter 4, 09_chapter 5, 10_annexures) on Shodhganga hdl 10603/596328
new_statements.locator: thesis pp. 193-194, sec. 9.2.1 'surlahar' (intonation) in sec. 9 'vakya-rachna (Syntax)'; = PDF pp. 112-113 (printed page = PDF page + 81); scanned files agarwal1963_07_chapter3_ocr_hin/; wording verified on the page images. Related passages: p. 166 (PDF p. 81, sec. 7.5.2), p. 192 (PDF p. 111), pp. 208-210 (PDF pp. 127-129, sec. 9.4), p. 220 ( PDF p. 5, sec. 10.2.1), p. 232 ( PDF p. 2, sec. 11.0)
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Shekhawati has an empty rule; the one existing statement is the 1964 book's p. 197 svarāghāt passage (read as 'unclear or contradictory'). The thesis carries that passage verbatim at p. 220 (sec. 10.2.1) and adds the missing context: in this description 'stress' is sentence emphasis on the focused word, the suprasegmentals of ch. 2 are intonation and juncture only, and no word-stress placement rule exists anywhere in the work. Compatible with what is recorded; it settles that the p. 197/220 passage is not a word-stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis treats 'stress' (balāghāt) only as sentence-level emphasis: it falls on the interrogative word if there is one, otherwise on whichever word the speaker puts in focus (the same sentence is shown with stress on the verb, the object and the subject). Intonation (falling for statements, rising for questions, drawn-out for exclamations) is the only other prosodic feature described. Nowhere in chapters 1, 3, 4, 5 or the annexures is there a statement of where stress or accent falls inside a word; 'accent' (svarāghāt) appears only at p. 166 (accent differs between participle+verb sequences and true compound verbs, e.g. vo roto jāve 'he goes crying' vs. 'he keeps crying') and p. 220 (the passage already on record: vowel shortening in derivatives/compounds is attributed to a change of accent position, without saying where the accent is).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Other exponents of emphasis noted: departure from the fixed word order (pp. 208-209, 'vo thāre sū̃ bāt karī' vs. 'karī vo thāre sū̃ bāt?') and the emphatic particles ī, bī, to, tak placed right after the emphasised word (p. 210). Sec. 9.2.1 (p. 192) and sec. 11.0 (p. 232) say the means/instruments for recording intonation and the finest pitch differences were not available, so only question/surprise/emphasis are illustrated and dialect geography is done at word level only.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Shekhawati of the Sikar–Jhunjhunu region (20 survey points mapped in the annexures) and distinguishes a western form (Marwari-influenced; past auxiliary ho/hā/hī) and an eastern form (tho/thā/thī; future in -go) in sec. 1.5.2; the stress remarks are not attributed to either sub-variety.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources: the only work opened is the thesis, and it is the same text as the already-checked 1964 book (Agrawal & Gupta), same author. Within the work there is an unreconciled tension: sec. 10.2.1 (p. 220 = book p. 197) attributes vowel shortening in derivatives to a change of 'accent positions' (implying word-level accent exists), while sec. 2.7 lists only intonation and juncture as suprasegmentals and sec. 9.2 treats stress purely as sentence emphasis; the thesis never states where word-level accent falls. The reading 'phrase-level prominence only' therefore records what the source describes, not a claim by the source that word stress is absent.
